analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from rejecting renters who pay with housing vouchers and penalizes neglect and vacant units.
analysis.headline: The Landlord Accountability Act died in committee with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added 'source of income' to the Fair Housing Act, so landlords could not refuse tenants just because they pay with a housing voucher, disability benefits, child support, or other lawful income. It would have imposed civil money penalties on landlords who deliberately let HUD-assisted units fall into disrepair to dodge program rules or who hold assisted multifamily units vacant for more than 60 days, created a federal complaint line and complaint-resolution program for tenants of assisted multifamily housing, funded tenant anti-harassment programs, and offered a tax credit to landlords who keep voucher-tenant buildings well maintained. It was referred to three House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who use Section 8 housing vouchers or receive Social Security, disability, or child-support income, who today can be turned away by 'no vouchers' policies; and tenants of HUD-assisted multifamily buildings, who would get a better-staffed complaint line, a formal complaint-resolution process, public disclosure of landlord complaints, and posted notices of their rights. Voucher holders often have few landlords willing to accept them; a national non-discrimination rule would multiply their housing options.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voucher holders and tenants in assisted housing

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'source of income' — including Section 8 vouchers, rental and homeownership subsidies, Social Security and disability benefits, and spousal or child support — as a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, with penalties for violations [S2] [S3].

Imposes a $100,000 civil money penalty per violation on owners who intentionally take or skip actions that make a unit too substandard to qualify for HUD assistance, and lets affected tenants sue for $50,000 plus actual damages [S3].
Penalizes owners of HUD-assisted multifamily units $100,000 for every 30 days a rentable unit is intentionally left vacant beyond 60 days, aimed at holding vacant assisted units off the market [S3].

Requires HUD to staff up the Multifamily Housing Complaint Line, create a complaint-resolution program for voucher users in multifamily housing, and publicly post each complaint and its disposition on a HUD website [S2] [S3].

Authorizes $25 million a year for fiscal 2024-2028 for grants to states, local governments, and nonprofits for tenant harassment prevention programs, including legal help for tenants facing landlords pressuring them to leave [S2] [S3].

Creates a maintenance tax credit for landlords of buildings with voucher tenants, worth up to $2,500 per unit and $500,000 per landlord per year, but only if complaints against them are resolved within 30 days [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rental property owners, especially owners of HUD-assisted multifamily buildings, who would face new penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, lose the ability to screen out voucher holders, and bear compliance costs. Federal taxpayers would fund the fair-housing enforcement grants, the complaint infrastructure, and the new landlord tax credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Landlords, especially multifamily owners, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The landlord tax credit is a real cost to the Treasury: it covers maintenance expenses landlords would arguably incur anyway, up to $500,000 per taxpayer per year, running through 2033 [S3].

The vacant-unit penalty of $100,000 for every 30 days could push owners to rent units before finishing renovations; the bill tries to manage this by presuming units under renovation are unavailable, but that presumption can be rebutted if a reasonable repair period has elapsed [S3].

Landlord and industry groups typically argue that a federal mandate overriding local screening rules and steep per-violation penalties raise compliance costs that get passed into rents; no such opposition appears in the record for this bill because no hearings were ever held.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — a national ban on 'no vouchers' discrimination and penalties for deliberately degrading assisted units — would meaningfully expand housing options for voucher holders, a group that faces widespread refusal by landlords. The main costs fall on landlords in the form of penalties and compliance, and on taxpayers through the enforcement grants and the maintenance tax credit; the tax credit is the weakest part of the design, since it subsidizes ordinary maintenance and is only available to landlords who avoid complaints. On balance the bill's benefits for low-income renters outweigh its costs, though its steep per-violation penalties would invite disputes over what counts as intentional neglect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees in March 2023, and none of them ever took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velázquez introduced the bill on March 7, 2023, and it was referred to the Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history [S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors over its two-year life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rental property owners and landlords are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to refuse voucher holders, face no federal penalties for vacant assisted units or degraded conditions, and the taxpayer-funded maintenance tax credit never became either a benefit or a constraint.

for.name: Fair housing and tenant advocacy organizations
for.what_they_did: Support the policies in this bill generally, such as source-of-income discrimination bans; the record contains no organized advocacy on this specific bill, which attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill's fair-housing amendment and liability provisions; no hearing or markup in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape is unknown; the sponsor was a Democrat and no Republican cosponsored it, but with zero cosponsors of any party the bill never became a party-line contest.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from refusing voucher holders, impose $100,000 penalties for intentionally degrading HUD-assisted units or holding them vacant, and require posted tenant-rights notices. It offsets some of that with a maintenance tax credit worth up to $500,000 a year for compliant owners of voucher-tenant buildings, but the tax break is conditional on clean complaint records.

industries.industry: Fair housing and tenant legal-services organizations
industries.note: The bill authorizes $90 million a year for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, $47 million a year for state fair-housing agencies, and $25 million a year for tenant harassment prevention grants, routing funds to nonprofits that counsel and represent tenants.

industries.industry: Property management and real estate services
industries.note: Source-of-income protection would apply across rental and real estate transactions, ending 'no voucher' and similar income screens as standard practice and adding complaint and compliance procedures.
